common_name: Kannah Creek Buckwheat (Compact Evergreen Sulphur-Flower Buckwheat)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in lean, gravelly, sharply drained soil in full sun; 'Kannah Creek' forms a tight, woody-based mat and resents heavy or wet soil far more than it minds heat or drought.

directions: Plant in lean, gravelly, very well-drained soil in full sun, mulching with rock or grit rather than bark to keep the crown dry. This selection, discovered along Kannah Creek on Colorado's Grand Mesa, forms a dense, low mat of rounded, felted gray-green leaves that turns rich burgundy and rust through fall and winter, giving the plant strong multi-season interest well beyond its bloom period. Wiry reddish stems carry tight clusters of small bright yellow flowers from late spring into summer, aging to a warm copper-rust as they fade, and the flowers are a magnet for native bees and other pollinators. It is exceptionally drought and heat tolerant once established, needs no fertilizer, and is well suited to rock gardens, gravel plantings, and dry slopes where richer groundcovers would fail.

common_name: Blue Spire Russian Sage (Upright Violet-Blue Russian Sage)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; 'Blue Spire' needs the same sharp drainage as the species and is prone to crown rot in heavy or poorly drained ground.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean soil in full sun; 'Blue Spire' is a selected Russian sage prized for its strong, sturdy, upright stems that hold the flower spikes erect without the flopping that can affect seed-grown plants. Deeply cut, aromatic, silver-gray foliage sets off dense, richly colored violet-blue flower spikes from midsummer well into fall, and the airy silhouette works equally well as a see-through screen or a hazy backdrop for bolder perennials. Like the species it is highly drought tolerant, deer and rabbit resistant, and attractive to bees once established, and it benefits from being cut back hard to a low framework each spring rather than fall to protect the crown through winter. Excellent drainage is the single most important factor for long-term survival, particularly in humid summer climates.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in lean, sandy, very well-drained soil in full sun; 'Silver Brocade' spreads by trailing stems that root as they go and rots quickly in heavy, wet, or richly amended soil.

directions: Plant in lean, sandy, very well-drained soil in full sun, giving the trailing stems room to spread since this selection roots readily where nodes touch the soil. 'Silver Brocade' stays lower and flatter than the species, forming a dense, prostrate carpet of deeply lobed, densely white-felted leaves that reads almost like scalloped fabric, and it rarely produces the small yellow flower clusters the species is known for, keeping the foliage display uninterrupted all season. Its tight, mat-forming habit makes it a favorite for edging paths, spilling over walls, and filling gaps between pavers in hot, sandy, or coastal gardens where salt spray and wind would damage less tolerant groundcovers. Trim back stray runners in spring to keep the mat tidy and prevent it from smothering neighboring plants.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: Mersea Yellow Pineleaf Penstemon (Yellow-Flowered Pineleaf Penstemon)

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery stock in spring into very well-drained, dry, gravelly, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun, matching the sharp-drainage needs of the species.

directions: Plant in gritty, sharply drained, lean soil in full sun, the same conditions required by the species; 'Mersea Yellow' is a color selection of pineleaf penstemon that replaces the typical scarlet-orange flowers with clear soft yellow, giving xeriscape and rock garden designers a rare warm-yellow, hummingbird-friendly penstemon for hot, dry sites. It keeps the same compact, mounding, evergreen habit and needle-like foliage as the species, blooming heavily from late spring through summer and reblooming after a light shearing. Pair it with orange- or red-flowered dryland companions for color contrast, or mass it alone for a long season of soft yellow bloom; it tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil but will not tolerate standing water or heavy, slow-draining ground.

planting.note: Plant container-grown offsets in spring in extremely well-drained, gritty or rocky soil in full sun to light afternoon shade in the hottest climates; perfect drainage is essential to prevent rot.

directions: Plant in extremely well-drained, gritty or rocky soil in full sun to light shade where summer sun is most intense; this compact, slow-growing selection of Agave potatorum forms a tight, symmetrical rosette of broad, undulate, blue-gray to gray-green leaves edged in irregular cream to white marginal bands and tipped with a stout reddish-brown terminal spine. Its name, sometimes rendered 'Kissho Kan,' translates roughly as 'lucky crown,' reflecting its status as one of the most sought-after small ornamental agave selections among succulent collectors. Like other agave it is essentially maintenance free once established, needing only occasional deep watering during extended drought and no fertilizer, and its compact size suits containers, rock gardens, and small courtyard plantings better than large agave species. It is monocarpic, flowering once after many years on a tall stalk before the rosette dies, typically leaving offsets behind.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

common_name: Route 66 California Fuchsia (Compact Orange-Red Hummingbird Trumpet)

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; 'Route 66' stays more compact and tidy than many California fuchsia selections while still spreading gradually by rhizome.

directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; 'Route 66' forms a dense, low mound of narrow, silvery-gray foliage that stays neater and more compact through the growing season than many other California fuchsia selections. From late summer into fall it produces an especially heavy show of large, brilliant orange-red tubular flowers held just above the foliage, timed to coincide with fall hummingbird migration when few other dry-climate perennials are still blooming. It is bred for wider cold hardiness than typical coastal California fuchsia forms, tolerating cold winters as well as heat and drought once established. Cut the whole plant back hard in late winter to remove the previous season's woody growth and encourage a fresh, dense flush of silvery foliage.
